newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Roche briefing comforts bullish analysts.
newsitem.headline: Roche briefing comforts bullish analysts.

text.p: Analysts came away from a product presentation by Roche Holding AG on Monday encouraged in their bullish views of the Swiss pharmaceuticals group.
At the full-day presentation at Roche's Basle headquarters company officials gave a broad overview of pharmaceutical drugs in the late and early stages of the research pipeline.
"It was a very positive and exciting meeting," said Genghis Lloyd-Harris, head of pharmaceuticals reseach at Credit Suisse First Boston (CSFB).
"Roche is already good, but they want to be better," said Meinrad Gyr of Zurich Kantonalbank.
"The meeting gave us a much better understanding of the long-term pipeline," a Zurich-based analyst said.
While many analysts were still busy digesting the wealth of scientific and technical information presented by Roche, some were already reviewing and planning to raise earnings forecasts.
On the stock market the briefing was well-received and Roche's non-voting equity securities continued to rocket.
At midsession Roche certificates were up 115 francs to 12,355 francs on a generally higher Swiss Exchange.
Since the start of this year Roche certificates have gained 18 percent, double the nine percent gain in the broad SPI index.
The rise has not only been fueled by speculative buying on merger and divestment rumours, but also by buying by long-term investors, analysts said.

Roche also confirmed at the meeting that 1996 and 1997 were transition years where earnings will tend to be burdened by the cost of developing new products. But from 1998 revenue from several new drugs will push up earnings.
In addition to presenting new drugs in the early stage of the research pipeline, Roche also used the briefing to convey its message of "development as a competitive weapon."
Roche plans to cut the fully-loaded cost of developing new drugs by 40 percent, or from an industry average of $500 million to $300 million.
"These are very aggressive figures, but given that Roche tends to be on the conservative side, I am comfortable," Lloyd-Harris said.
Research spending as a percentage of pharmaceutical revenue is planned to be reduced to 18 percent by year 2000 from around 21 percent last year, an analyst said.
Half of the cost savings will come from process improvement and the other half from early elimination of unsuccessful drugs, a Roche spokesman confirmed.
In order to identify the potential market failures early-on, Roche managers will meet monthly to review progress within the global research programmes and market developments.
The improvement in the development process will come from a combination of four factors: Cost efficiency, speed, flexibility and innovation.
The average development time of drugs, for example, should be cut to four years from 5.6 years, Gyr said.
Among the drugs in the late-stage development that Roche presented were Posicor (a drug against hypertension), Xenical (against obesity) and Tasmar (treatment for Parkinson's disease).

Roche repeated its forecast for annual sales of Posicor of at least $800 million in year five after the drug's launch. Annual sales for Xenical are estimated at $700 million or more and sales of Tasmar at $500 million or more.
